title: Kerberoastable Accounts Found
description: {...} user account(s) have Service Principal Names (SPNs) set, making them vulnerable to Kerberoasting attacks. An attacker with any domain user credential can request TGS tickets for these accounts and crack them offline.
impact: Kerberoasting allows any authenticated domain user to request service tickets for SPN-bearing accounts and attempt offline password cracking. If the account password is weak, the attacker obtains the cleartext credential. Privileged service accounts (e.g., SQL service accounts in Domain Admins) are especially high-value targets.
remediation_brief: Set strong, complex passwords (25+ characters) on all accounts with SPNs. Migrate service accounts to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) which rotate passwords automatically. Remove unnecessary SPNs. Monitor for anomalous TGS-REQ activity (Event ID 4769).

title: AS-REP Roastable Accounts Found
description: {...} account(s) have Kerberos pre-authentication disabled (DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag). These accounts are vulnerable to AS-REP roasting, allowing offline password cracking without any prior authentication.
impact: AS-REP roasting is more dangerous than Kerberoasting because it does not require any valid domain credentials to execute. An attacker can request encrypted AS-REP messages for these accounts from outside the domain and crack them offline. This is a common initial access technique in Active Directory attacks.
remediation_brief: Enable Kerberos pre-authentication on all accounts: clear the 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication' checkbox in account properties. No legitimate scenario requires this flag for standard user accounts. Audit accounts regularly for this flag. Monitor for anomalous AS-REQ traffic (Event ID 4768 with pre-auth type 0).

title: Unconstrained Delegation Configured
description: {...} non-domain-controller account(s) are configured for unconstrained Kerberos delegation. These systems can impersonate any user that authenticates to them, including domain administrators.
impact: Unconstrained delegation allows a compromised server to reuse any user's Kerberos TGT that was forwarded during authentication. An attacker who compromises a server with unconstrained delegation can capture domain admin TGTs and use them to fully compromise the domain. This is a critical privilege escalation path in Active Directory environments.
remediation_brief: Replace unconstrained delegation with constrained delegation or resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD). Add privileged accounts to the Protected Users group or mark them as 'Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated'. Only Domain Controllers should have unconstrained delegation.

title: Weak Domain Password Policy
description: The domain password policy does not meet security best practices. Minimum password length, complexity requirements, or password history may be insufficient, allowing users to set weak or commonly guessed passwords.
impact: A weak domain password policy applies to all domain user accounts. Short passwords without complexity requirements can be cracked rapidly via offline attacks against NTDS.dit or captured hashes. The domain password policy is the single most impactful password control in the environment.
remediation_brief: Increase minimum password length to 12+ characters (14+ for privileged accounts). Enable complexity requirements. Set maximum password age to 60-90 days. Enforce at least 12 passwords of history. Deploy Fine-Grained Password Policies (PSOs) for privileged tiers. Implement Azure AD Password Protection for banned password lists.

title: LDAP Signing Not Enforced
description: LDAP signing is set to '{...}' instead of 'Require signing'. This allows LDAP traffic to be transmitted unsigned, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks.
impact: Without enforced LDAP signing, an attacker can perform LDAP relay attacks, intercepting and modifying LDAP queries and responses. This can be used to escalate privileges, modify group memberships, or reset passwords via LDAP relay combined with NTLM relay techniques (e.g., ntlmrelayx).
remediation_brief: Set 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' to 'Require signing' via Group Policy. Also enable LDAP channel binding. Test thoroughly before enforcement as it may break legacy applications using simple LDAP binds.

title: Kerberos DES Encryption Enabled on Accounts
description: The domain supports weak Kerberos encryption types: {...}. DES and RC4 are cryptographically broken and should not be used for Kerberos authentication.
impact: DES-encrypted Kerberos tickets can be cracked trivially. RC4-HMAC (NTLM-based) is vulnerable to Kerberoasting offline cracking and overpass-the-hash attacks. Allowing weak encryption types downgrades the security of the entire Kerberos infrastructure.
remediation_brief: Disable DES and RC4 encryption types in the domain. Set msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes to support only AES128 (0x08) and AES256 (0x10). Test thoroughly — legacy systems (especially pre-2008 R2) may require RC4. Migrate legacy systems before disabling.

title: Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) Configured
description: {...} account(s) have Resource-Based Constrained Delegation configured (msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity). RBCD allows specified principals to impersonate users to the target service.
impact: RBCD is a common privilege escalation vector. If an attacker can write to the msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute of a target (via WRITE permission on the computer object), they can configure RBCD to impersonate any user (including Domain Admin) to that target's services. This is the basis of the RBCD/S4U2Self/S4U2Proxy attack chain.
remediation_brief: Review all RBCD configurations for legitimacy. Ensure that only authorized principals have WRITE access to computer objects' msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute. Monitor changes to this attribute via Event ID 5136. Remove unnecessary RBCD configurations.

title: Domain Functional Level Outdated
description: The Active Directory domain or forest functional level is below the current recommended level for the installed domain controller OS version. Outdated functional levels prevent the use of modern security features such as Protected Users group, Authentication Policies, and Kerberos armoring.
impact: Outdated functional levels prevent the use of modern Active Directory security features including: Protected Users group (2012 R2+), Authentication Policies and Silos (2012 R2+), gMSA improvements, Kerberos armoring (FAST), and AES-only Kerberos enforcement. Older levels also correspond to operating systems that may be end-of-life.
remediation_brief: Raise the domain and forest functional levels after ensuring all Domain Controllers are running a supported Windows Server version. This is a one-way operation — test in a lab environment first. Target at minimum Windows Server 2016 functional level.

title: AdminSDHolder Orphaned Protected Accounts
description: {...} account(s) have AdminCount=1 set but are not current members of any privileged group. These are orphaned AdminSDHolder protections from former privilege.
impact: Orphaned AdminSDHolder flags indicate accounts that were previously in privileged groups. The AdminCount flag persists after removal, and the AdminSDHolder ACL propagation may have left non-standard permissions. Attackers target these accounts as they may retain residual privileges or weaker ACLs.
remediation_brief: Clear the AdminCount attribute on accounts no longer in privileged groups. Reset the ACL on these accounts to inherit from the parent OU. Use the AdminSDHolder cleanup script to automate this process. Monitor AdminCount changes with Event ID 5136.

title: HIGH
description: A browser extension matching known malicious or data-exfiltrating extensions was detected.
impact: Malicious browser extensions can steal credentials, intercept all web traffic, inject ads, redirect searches, exfiltrate cookies and session tokens, and modify web page content. They operate with the user's full browsing context.
remediation_brief: Remove the malicious extension immediately from all affected browser profiles. Clear browsing data including cookies and saved passwords. Change passwords for any accounts accessed while the extension was active. Implement browser extension management via Group Policy to whitelist approved extensions only.

title: MEDIUM
description: A browser extension was detected that is not in the known-good extension database and cannot be verified as legitimate.
impact: Unknown extensions may have been sideloaded or installed from untrusted sources. They could contain hidden data collection, credential stealing, or ad injection capabilities that are not immediately apparent.
remediation_brief: Review the extension's permissions, source, and publisher. If the extension cannot be verified as legitimate and necessary, remove it. Implement extension management policies that restrict installation to approved extensions from official stores only.

title: MEDIUM
description: An installed browser is not at the latest major version and may be missing critical security patches.
impact: Browsers are a primary attack vector for drive-by downloads and phishing. Outdated browsers miss critical patches for JavaScript engine bugs, rendering vulnerabilities, and sandbox escapes that enable remote code execution.
remediation_brief: Update all browsers to their latest stable versions. Enable automatic browser updates. For enterprise environments, use WSUS, SCCM, or browser-specific enterprise management tools to deploy updates centrally.

title: Expired Certificate
description: One or more certificates in the local machine or current user certificate store have expired.
impact: Expired certificates cause service disruptions, authentication failures, and trust warnings. They may also indicate neglected systems or processes. Expired certificates used for code signing or SSL/TLS expose users to man-in-the-middle and substitution attacks.
remediation_brief: Renew or replace all expired certificates. Remove expired certificates that are no longer needed. Implement certificate lifecycle management with automated renewal alerts at 30, 14, and 7 days before expiry.

title: Certificate Expiring Soon
description: One or more certificates will expire within the next 30 days.
impact: Certificates expiring soon risk service disruptions if not renewed in time. SSL/TLS certificate expiry causes browser warnings and connection failures. Authentication certificate expiry can lock out users.
remediation_brief: Renew expiring certificates before their expiry date. Use automated certificate management tools (ACME, internal CA auto-enrollment) where possible. Verify new certificates are properly installed and tested before the old ones expire.

title: Self-Signed Certificate in Trust Store
description: Certificates using deprecated signature algorithms (SHA1) or insufficient key lengths (RSA < 2048 bits) were detected.
impact: SHA1 signatures are vulnerable to collision attacks, enabling certificate forgery. RSA keys shorter than 2048 bits can be factored with sufficient computational resources, compromising the certificate's security.
remediation_brief: Replace weak certificates with ones using SHA-256 or stronger signature algorithms and RSA 2048-bit or longer keys (or ECDSA P-256+). Update internal CA templates to enforce modern cryptographic standards.

title: Weak Certificate Signature Algorithm
description: A self-signed certificate that is not from a well-known Certificate Authority was found in the Trusted Root Certification Authorities store.
impact: Unknown root certificates in the trusted store could enable man-in-the-middle attacks by allowing an attacker's CA to issue trusted certificates for any domain. This could be from legitimate enterprise CA deployment or from malware installing rogue roots.
remediation_brief: Review all non-standard root certificates. Verify each against the organization's internal CA infrastructure. Remove any certificates that cannot be accounted for. If a rogue root is found, investigate how it was installed and treat the system as potentially compromised.

title: Weak Certificate Key Size
description: A certificate using a key size shorter than 2048 bits was detected. Keys shorter than 2048 bits are considered weak and can be factored with modern computing resources, compromising all protections the certificate provides.
impact: A weak key can be factored using distributed computing or cloud resources. 1024-bit RSA keys have been publicly factored, and NIST deprecated keys shorter than 2048 bits since 2013. An attacker who factors the key can forge signatures, decrypt traffic, and impersonate the certificate holder.
remediation_brief: Replace the certificate with one using at least a 2048-bit RSA key (3072-bit or 4096-bit recommended for long-lived certificates). For new deployments, consider ECDSA P-256 or P-384 keys which provide equivalent security at smaller sizes. Update the certificate on all services and endpoints.

title: Firewall Profile Disabled
description: The endpoint's configuration passes fewer than 50% of applicable CIS Benchmark controls, indicating severe hardening deficiencies.
impact: Below 50% CIS compliance represents a fundamentally unhardened system with numerous security weaknesses. The system is significantly more vulnerable to common attack techniques than a properly hardened baseline.
remediation_brief: Develop a system hardening plan based on the CIS Benchmark for the specific Windows version. Prioritize Level 1 controls first as they have minimal operational impact. Implement changes through Group Policy for consistent deployment across endpoints.

title: Screen Lock Timeout Not Configured
description: The endpoint passes between 50% and 80% of applicable CIS Benchmark controls, indicating room for improvement in system hardening.
impact: While partially hardened, the system has notable security gaps that could be exploited. Each unaddressed CIS control represents a specific attack vector that an adversary could leverage.
remediation_brief: Address the specific failing CIS controls, prioritizing those related to authentication, access control, and network security. Focus on Level 1 controls that have not been implemented. Use Group Policy to enforce configurations across the organization.

title: NetBIOS over TCP/IP Enabled
description: Category I DISA STIG findings (high severity) are present, representing vulnerabilities that could directly lead to system compromise.
impact: STIG CAT I findings represent the most critical security weaknesses. They typically allow unauthorized access, denial of service, or information disclosure with high impact. DoD and many other organizations require zero CAT I findings for system accreditation.
remediation_brief: Remediate all DISA STIG Category I findings immediately. These represent the highest priority security issues. Apply STIG fixes via Group Policy or SCAP compliance tools. Document any findings requiring a Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) if immediate remediation is not possible.

title: IPv6 Transition Technologies Enabled
description: Category II DISA STIG findings (medium severity) are present, representing security weaknesses that could contribute to system compromise.
impact: STIG CAT II findings are significant security weaknesses that, while not immediately critical, contribute to an insecure posture and may be combined with other findings to achieve compromise. Organizations typically require CAT II remediation within 90 days.
remediation_brief: Plan remediation of DISA STIG Category II findings within 90 days. Prioritize those related to authentication and access control. Apply STIG fixes via Group Policy where possible for consistent deployment.

title: Remote Registry Service Enabled
description: An aggregate endpoint hardening score was calculated based on all security checks performed, providing an overall security posture assessment.
impact: The hardening score provides a quantitative measure of the endpoint's security configuration. A low score indicates multiple security weaknesses that collectively increase the risk of compromise, while a high score indicates a well-hardened system.
remediation_brief: Use the hardening score as a baseline measurement and track improvements over time. Prioritize remediation of findings that contribute most to the score deficit. Establish a target hardening score and implement a continuous improvement program.

title: Brute Force Attack Detected
description: Brute-force login activity detected with multiple failed authentication attempts from the same source within the past 7 days. Sources with more than 10 failures indicate automated credential guessing attacks targeting the system.
impact: Sustained brute-force attacks may eventually succeed, especially against accounts with weak or reused passwords. Successful compromise grants the attacker interactive access to the system and may lead to lateral movement, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration.
remediation_brief: Implement account lockout policies (5-10 attempts), enable multi-factor authentication, and block offending source IPs at the firewall. Investigate targeted accounts for compromise indicators. Consider implementing Azure AD Smart Lockout for adaptive protection.

title: Account Lockouts Detected
description: Account lockout events (Event ID 4740) were detected in the security event log, indicating accounts are being locked due to repeated failed authentication. Lockouts may be caused by brute-force attacks, misconfigured services, or stale cached credentials.
impact: Account lockouts from brute-force attempts confirm active credential attacks against the system. Service account lockouts can cause application outages and business disruption.
remediation_brief: Investigate the source of lockouts for each affected account. For user accounts, verify no credential compromise occurred. For service accounts, check for stale cached credentials in scheduled tasks, services, or mapped drives. Consider migrating to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA).

title: Security Log Cleared — Evidence Tampering
description: Event log clearing events detected (Event ID 1102/104). Clearing security logs destroys forensic evidence and is a strong indicator of attacker activity or insider threat attempting to cover their tracks.
impact: Cleared security logs eliminate the audit trail of authentication events, privilege escalation, and policy changes, preventing incident investigation and regulatory compliance verification. This is a common anti-forensics technique.
remediation_brief: Investigate the account that cleared the logs for compromise. Configure event log forwarding to a SIEM to preserve logs centrally. Restrict log management permissions to dedicated admin accounts. Enable alerting on Event ID 1102.

title: Suspicious PowerShell Activity in Event Logs
description: PowerShell events contain suspicious patterns including encoded commands (-EncodedCommand), download cradles (Invoke-WebRequest/IEX), AMSI bypass attempts, or known offensive tool invocations such as Mimikatz or PowerView.
impact: Suspicious PowerShell activity may indicate post-exploitation activity, malware execution, or attacker reconnaissance. PowerShell is the most commonly abused living-off-the-land tool on Windows systems.
remediation_brief: Investigate each suspicious PowerShell event. Check the executing user and originating process. Enable PowerShell ScriptBlock Logging, Transcription, and Constrained Language Mode. Consider deploying AppLocker or WDAC to restrict PowerShell usage to authorized administrators.

title: New Service Installations Detected
description: New service installation events (Event ID 7045/4697) recorded in event logs. Service installations are a common persistence mechanism used by malware and attackers to maintain access that survives reboots.
impact: Attackers install malicious services to maintain persistent access. Services run with elevated privileges and can be configured to start automatically, ensuring the attacker's code runs at every boot.
remediation_brief: Review each new service installation for legitimacy. Verify the service executable path, signing status, and the account used for installation. Remove unauthorized services and investigate how they were installed.

title: User Account Created
description: User account creation events (Event ID 4720) detected in security event logs. Account creation outside of normal provisioning workflows may indicate persistence or unauthorized access by an attacker.
impact: Attackers create local accounts to maintain persistent access. Unauthorized accounts may be added to privileged groups to escalate privileges and maintain a foothold on the compromised system.
remediation_brief: Verify each account creation was authorized through the proper provisioning workflow. Remove unauthorized accounts. Monitor for group membership changes (Event ID 4732) on newly created accounts.

title: UAC Disabled
description: User Account Control (UAC) is completely disabled on this endpoint. The registry value EnableLUA under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System is set to 0.
impact: All applications run with full administrative privileges without prompting. Malware and exploit payloads execute with elevated privileges immediately upon infection, greatly increasing the severity of any compromise.
remediation_brief: Re-enable UAC by setting the EnableLUA registry value to 1 at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System. Set ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin to at least 2 (prompt for consent on secure desktop). Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > User Account Control.

title: UAC Prompt Behavior Weak
description: The UAC elevation prompt for administrators is configured to auto-elevate without prompting (ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin is 0) or to prompt on a non-secure desktop.
impact: Weak UAC prompt settings allow malware to silently elevate privileges through auto-elevation or intercept elevation prompts on the interactive desktop, enabling privilege escalation without user awareness.
remediation_brief: Configure ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin to 2 (prompt for consent on the secure desktop) via Group Policy or registry. Also ensure PromptOnSecureDesktop is set to 1 to prevent interception of the elevation dialog by malicious software.

title: SMBv1 Protocol Enabled
description: The deprecated SMBv1 protocol is enabled on this endpoint, either as a server or client component.
impact: SMBv1 has known critical vulnerabilities including EternalBlue (MS17-010) and lacks modern security features. It enables remote code execution, credential relay attacks, and was the primary propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya ransomware.
remediation_brief: Disable SMBv1 by running: Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol. For Server: Remove-WindowsFeature FS-SMB1. Alternatively set HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters\SMB1 to 0. Verify no legacy applications or devices require SMBv1 before disabling.

title: SMB Signing Not Required
description: SMB message signing is not required on this endpoint, allowing unsigned SMB communications.
impact: Without mandatory SMB signing, an attacker in a man-in-the-middle position can intercept and modify SMB traffic, perform relay attacks (NTLM relay), and hijack authenticated SMB sessions to access file shares or execute commands on other systems.
remediation_brief: Enable mandatory SMB signing by setting RequireSecuritySignature to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters and LanmanWorkstation\Parameters. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Microsoft network server/client: Digitally sign communications (always).

title: NTLMv1 Authentication Allowed
description: The LAN Manager authentication level allows NTLMv1 responses, a weak authentication protocol that is trivially crackable.
impact: NTLMv1 hashes can be cracked in seconds using rainbow tables or GPU-accelerated attacks, exposing user passwords. An attacker capturing NTLMv1 traffic on the network can recover plaintext credentials for lateral movement.
remediation_brief: Set LmCompatibilityLevel to 5 (Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM) at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Network security: LAN Manager authentication level. Test thoroughly as legacy devices may require NTLMv1.

title: LM Password Hashes Stored
description: The system is configured to store LAN Manager (LM) hash values for passwords, a severely weak hash format.
impact: LM hashes split passwords into two 7-character halves, are case-insensitive, and use DES without salt. They can be cracked in minutes even for complex passwords, giving an attacker who obtains the SAM database or captures authentication traffic immediate access to plaintext passwords.
remediation_brief: Set NoLMHash to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa to prevent storage of LM hashes. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change. Force all users to change passwords after enabling.

title: AutoRun Enabled
description: AutoRun/AutoPlay is enabled, allowing automatic execution of programs from removable media and network drives.
impact: Malware can be automatically executed when a USB drive, CD/DVD, or network share is accessed. This is a classic initial access vector used by worms (Conficker) and targeted attacks using planted USB devices.
remediation_brief: Set NoDriveTypeAutoRun to 255 (0xFF) at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer to disable AutoRun on all drive types. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > AutoPlay Policies > Turn off Autoplay (All drives).

title: WDigest Plaintext Credentials Enabled
description: WDigest authentication is configured to store plaintext credentials in memory (UseLogonCredential set to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest).
impact: An attacker who achieves local administrator access can use tools like Mimikatz to extract plaintext passwords from LSASS process memory for all currently logged-in users, including domain administrators. This enables immediate lateral movement without any cracking.
remediation_brief: Set UseLogonCredential to 0 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest. On Windows 8.1/Server 2012 R2 and later with KB2871997 installed, WDigest plaintext caching is disabled by default. Verify the registry value is explicitly set to 0 to prevent re-enablement by malware.

title: LSA Protection Not Enabled
description: Local Security Authority (LSA) protection is not enabled. The RunAsPPL registry value is not set to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa.
impact: Without LSA protection, the LSASS process can be accessed by any process running as local administrator. Attackers can dump credentials from LSASS memory using standard tools, bypassing most endpoint security controls.
remediation_brief: Enable LSA protection by setting RunAsPPL to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. A system restart is required. Test application compatibility first as some security products may not function with PPL enabled. On Windows 11 22H2+, LSA protection is enabled by default.

title: Credential Guard Not Enabled
description: Windows Defender Credential Guard (Virtualization Based Security for credential isolation) is not enabled on this endpoint.
impact: Without Credential Guard, NTLM hashes and Kerberos TGTs stored in LSASS memory can be extracted by tools running as local administrator. Credential Guard isolates these secrets in a hardware-backed virtual enclave that even kernel-level attackers cannot access.
remediation_brief: Enable Credential Guard by setting EnableVirtualizationBasedSecurity to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\DeviceGuard and RequirePlatformSecurityFeatures to 1 or 3. Prerequisites: UEFI firmware, Secure Boot, TPM 2.0, and 64-bit Windows 10/11 Enterprise or Server 2016+. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Device Guard.

title: LLMNR Enabled
description: Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) is enabled, allowing unauthenticated name resolution on the local network.
impact: An attacker on the local network can respond to LLMNR queries to capture NTLMv2 hashes from connecting clients using tools like Responder. These hashes can be cracked offline or relayed to other services for unauthorized access.
remediation_brief: Disable LLMNR via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client > Turn off multicast name resolution. Set EnableMulticast to 0 at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\DNSClient. Ensure proper DNS infrastructure is in place as a replacement.

title: WPAD Enabled
description: Web Proxy Auto-Discovery (WPAD) protocol is enabled, allowing automatic proxy configuration via DNS or DHCP.
impact: An attacker can poison WPAD queries via LLMNR/NBNS or rogue DHCP to redirect all HTTP traffic through a malicious proxy, enabling credential interception, session hijacking, and man-in-the-middle attacks on all web traffic.
remediation_brief: Disable the WinHTTP Auto-Proxy Service (WinHttpAutoProxySvc) and set its startup to Disabled. In Internet Options, uncheck 'Automatically detect settings'. If proxy auto-configuration is needed, use explicit PAC file URLs rather than WPAD discovery.

title: PowerShell Script Block Logging Disabled
description: PowerShell script block logging is not enabled, preventing the recording of PowerShell script content in Windows Event Logs.
impact: Without script block logging, PowerShell-based attacks (obfuscated download cradles, in-memory execution, AMSI bypasses) leave no forensic evidence. Incident response teams cannot determine what malicious PowerShell commands were executed.
remediation_brief: Enable PowerShell script block logging via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging. Set EnableScriptBlockLogging to 1 at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging.

title: PowerShell Module Logging Disabled
description: PowerShell module logging is not enabled, which would record pipeline execution details for specified modules.
impact: Module logging provides a detailed record of which PowerShell cmdlets and functions were invoked. Without it, forensic investigators have reduced visibility into the specific operations performed during an attack.
remediation_brief: Enable PowerShell module logging via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on Module Logging. Configure the module names to log (use * for all modules).

title: PowerShell Transcription Disabled
description: PowerShell transcription (recording of all PowerShell input and output to text files) is not enabled.
impact: Transcription provides a complete record of interactive and scripted PowerShell sessions including output. Without it, defenders lose a valuable forensic data source for investigating PowerShell-based attacks.
remediation_brief: Enable PowerShell transcription via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on PowerShell Transcription. Configure the output directory to a secured file share for centralized collection. Ensure adequate disk space and proper NTFS permissions on the transcript directory.

title: PowerShell v2 Engine Available
description: The PowerShell v2 engine is still installed as a Windows feature, providing a downgrade path that bypasses modern logging and security controls.
impact: Attackers can invoke PowerShell v2 (powershell -version 2) to bypass AMSI, script block logging, constrained language mode, and other security features that only exist in PowerShell v5+. This is a well-documented defense evasion technique.
remediation_brief: Remove the PowerShell v2 engine: Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2Root. For Server: Remove-WindowsFeature PowerShell-V2. Verify no applications depend on PowerShell v2 before removal.

title: Windows Defender Disabled
description: Windows Defender Antivirus is completely disabled or not running on this endpoint with no alternative antimalware solution detected.
impact: Without antimalware protection, all known malware including commodity threats, ransomware, and trojans can execute without detection. The system has no real-time file scanning, web filtering, or behavior monitoring.
remediation_brief: Re-enable Windows Defender by removing any Group Policy that disables it (DisableAntiSpyware registry key), starting the WinDefend service, and ensuring real-time protection is turned on. If a third-party antivirus is intended, verify it is properly installed and running. Ensure at minimum one antimalware solution is active at all times.

title: Windows Defender Exclusions Present
description: Windows Defender has file, folder, process, or extension exclusions configured that exempt certain paths or processes from scanning.
impact: Attackers frequently target known exclusion paths to stage and execute malware. Common exclusion paths like temp directories, development folders, or application paths become safe havens for malicious payloads that will never be scanned.
remediation_brief: Review all Windows Defender exclusions and remove any that are not strictly necessary for application compatibility. Document the business justification for each remaining exclusion. Avoid broad exclusions (entire drives, common directories). Monitor excluded paths for suspicious file creation via separate detection mechanisms.

title: Windows Defender Real-Time Protection Off
description: Windows Defender is installed but real-time protection is turned off, leaving the system without active file scanning.
impact: Files downloaded, copied, or created are not scanned until a manual or scheduled scan occurs. Malware can execute immediately upon arrival without triggering any detection, potentially running for hours or days before a scheduled scan.
remediation_brief: Enable real-time protection in Windows Security settings or via PowerShell: Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $false. If Group Policy is preventing this, update the policy to allow real-time protection. Verify protection is active with Get-MpComputerStatus.

title: Remote Desktop Without NLA
description: Remote Desktop Protocol is enabled without requiring Network Level Authentication (NLA), allowing unauthenticated users to reach the RDP login screen.
impact: Without NLA, attackers can establish RDP sessions without credentials, consuming server resources (DoS) and reaching the Windows login screen where they can attempt credential attacks. This also exposes the system to pre-authentication RDP vulnerabilities like BlueKeep.
remediation_brief: Enable NLA for Remote Desktop by setting UserAuthentication to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Remote Desktop Services > Remote Desktop Session Host > Security > Require user authentication for remote connections by using Network Level Authentication.

title: DEP Not Enabled System-Wide
description: Data Execution Prevention (DEP) is not configured to protect all programs, only essential Windows programs and services.
impact: Without system-wide DEP, buffer overflow exploits can execute shellcode in data memory regions. DEP prevents code execution from non-executable memory pages, making many common exploitation techniques significantly harder.
remediation_brief: Configure DEP to protect all programs by running: bcdedit /set nx AlwaysOn. Alternatively, configure via System Properties > Advanced > Performance Settings > Data Execution Prevention > Turn on DEP for all programs and services except those I select. Add specific exceptions only for applications that are confirmed incompatible.

title: Anonymous Access to Named Pipes
description: Anonymous (null session) access to named pipes is permitted, allowing unauthenticated users to connect to specific named pipes on the system.
impact: Attackers can enumerate sensitive information through named pipes without authentication, including user lists, group memberships, share lists, and security policies. This information aids in planning targeted credential attacks and privilege escalation.
remediation_brief: Clear the NullSessionPipes registry value at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters and set RestrictNullSessAccess to 1. Apply via Group Policy: Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares (Enabled).

title: Null Session Access Allowed
description: The system allows null session (anonymous) connections for SAM enumeration and share enumeration.
impact: Attackers can connect without credentials to enumerate all user accounts, groups, and network shares. This provides a complete map of the attack surface and user accounts to target for password spraying or brute force attacks.
remediation_brief: Set RestrictAnonymousSAM to 1 and RestrictAnonymous to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. Apply via Group Policy: Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts (Enabled) and Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares (Enabled).

title: Audit Policy Insufficient
description: The Windows audit policy does not log critical security events. Key audit categories such as logon events, privilege use, object access, or policy changes are not configured for success and/or failure auditing.
impact: Without comprehensive audit logging, security incidents go undetected and uninvestigated. Login attempts, privilege escalation, file access, and policy changes occur without any record, severely impacting incident response and forensic capabilities.
remediation_brief: Configure advanced audit policy via Group Policy to log at minimum: Logon/Logoff (Success+Failure), Account Logon (Success+Failure), Privilege Use (Success+Failure), Object Access (Failure), Policy Change (Success+Failure), System (Success+Failure). Use auditpol to verify: auditpol /get /category:*.

title: Print Spooler Running on Server
description: The Print Spooler service is running on a server where printing functionality is likely not required.
impact: The Print Spooler service has been the target of multiple critical vulnerabilities including PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) enabling remote code execution and privilege escalation. Running it on servers unnecessarily increases the attack surface.
remediation_brief: Disable the Print Spooler service on servers that do not need printing: Stop-Service -Name Spooler -Force; Set-Service -Name Spooler -StartupType Disabled. On domain controllers, the Spooler should always be disabled as it exposes the DC to coercion attacks via the MS-RPRN protocol.

title: Suspicious Outbound Connection Detected
description: The Windows Firewall is disabled for the Domain network profile.
impact: All inbound and outbound traffic is unfiltered when connected to a domain network. Any service listening on any port is exposed to all hosts on the network, enabling lateral movement and direct exploitation.
remediation_brief: Enable the Windows Firewall for the Domain profile via Group Policy or PowerShell: Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain -Enabled True. Review and configure appropriate inbound/outbound rules before enabling to avoid disrupting legitimate services.

title: High-Risk Port Exposed
description: The Windows Firewall is disabled for the Private network profile.
impact: All network traffic is unfiltered when connected to private networks. Services and ports that should be restricted are accessible to all devices on the local network segment.
remediation_brief: Enable the Windows Firewall for the Private profile: Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Private -Enabled True.

title: System Proxy Configured
description: The Windows Firewall is disabled for the Public network profile, the most exposed profile.
impact: When connected to any public or untrusted network (airports, hotels, coffee shops), all services are exposed without any filtering. This is the highest-risk firewall misconfiguration as public networks are inherently hostile.
remediation_brief: Immediately enable the Windows Firewall for the Public profile: Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Public -Enabled True. The Public profile should have the most restrictive ruleset with all inbound connections blocked by default.

title: DNS Pointing to External Servers on Domain-Joined System
description: A high-risk network port is listening on this endpoint (e.g., 445/SMB, 135-139/RPC, 3389/RDP, 23/Telnet, 21/FTP, 1433/MSSQL, 3306/MySQL, 5432/PostgreSQL).
impact: High-risk ports are frequent targets for automated scanning and exploitation. Exposed database ports enable direct SQL injection and credential brute-forcing. Exposed management ports enable remote administration attacks.
remediation_brief: Close or restrict access to unnecessary high-risk ports using Windows Firewall rules. For required services, restrict inbound access to specific authorized IP ranges. Consider using IPsec or VPN for administrative access to sensitive services.

title: Known Malicious Process Detected
description: One or more running processes match known malicious software signatures in the threat intelligence database. This is a strong indicator of active system compromise requiring immediate incident response.
impact: Known malicious processes indicate active malware execution. Depending on the malware type (RAT, keylogger, cryptominer, ransomware dropper), the attacker may have full remote access, be exfiltrating data, or preparing for destructive action. The system should be considered compromised.
remediation_brief: Immediately isolate the system from the network. Capture memory and disk images for forensic analysis before remediation. Identify the malware family and check for persistence mechanisms (scheduled tasks, services, registry run keys, WMI subscriptions). Re-image the system after forensics are complete.

title: Process Running from Temporary Directory
description: One or more processes are executing from temporary directories (%TEMP%, %TMP%, C:\Windows\Temp). Legitimate software rarely runs from temp folders; this pattern is a strong indicator of malware, dropper activity, or exploitation payload execution.
impact: Malware commonly stages and executes from temporary directories because they are user-writable, loosely monitored, and files there are expected to be transient. Ransomware droppers, fileless malware stagers, and post-exploitation payloads frequently use temp paths as their execution location.
remediation_brief: Investigate each process: check file hash against VirusTotal, examine parent process chain, check for associated network connections. Implement AppLocker or WDAC policies to block executable execution from temp directories. Enable Windows Defender ASR rules to block execution from temp paths.

title: Process with No Executable Path
description: One or more running processes have no associated executable path on disk. This may indicate fileless malware executing entirely from memory, process hollowing, or a process whose binary was deleted after execution.
impact: Processes without a disk-backed executable path can indicate fileless malware executing entirely from memory, process hollowing (where a legitimate process is replaced in memory with malicious code), or an attacker who deleted the binary after launching it to hinder forensic analysis.
remediation_brief: Investigate each process: capture a memory dump for forensic analysis, check the parent process chain for suspicious lineage, examine loaded DLLs and handles. Implement Sysmon with process creation logging (Event ID 1) to capture full command lines and parent process details.

title: SYSTEM Process Running from User-Writable Path
description: One or more processes are running as SYSTEM from user-writable locations (Users, AppData, Downloads, ProgramData, Temp). Legitimate SYSTEM processes run from protected directories (System32, Program Files). This is a strong indicator of privilege escalation or malware with elevated privileges.
impact: A process running as SYSTEM from a user-writable directory indicates successful privilege escalation. The attacker has achieved the highest local privilege level and can install rootkits, create backdoor accounts, modify security settings, access any file on the system, and pivot to other systems.
remediation_brief: Immediately investigate: capture memory and disk forensics, identify the privilege escalation vector (service binary hijacking, DLL search order hijacking, unquoted service path). Fix the underlying vulnerability. Deploy WDAC/AppLocker to prevent execution from user-writable paths.

title: Unauthorized Remote Management Tool Detected
description: A remote management tool (TeamViewer, AnyDesk, LogMeIn, ConnectWise, Splashtop, etc.) was detected that is not part of the organization's approved toolset.
impact: Unauthorized remote access tools create unmonitored backdoors into the network. They bypass VPN, firewall, and network security controls by tunneling through standard HTTPS. Attackers frequently install these tools for persistent remote access.
remediation_brief: Remove unauthorized remote management tools and block their installation via application control policies. If the tool was installed by an attacker, initiate incident response. Maintain an approved remote access solution with centralized logging and multi-factor authentication.

title: RDP Enabled
description: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) is enabled on this system. RDP exposes the system to brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, and known RDP vulnerabilities including BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) and DejaBlue.
impact: An attacker who gains RDP access obtains full interactive control of the system. Without NLA, unauthenticated attackers can reach the login screen and exploit pre-authentication vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: Disable RDP if not required. If required, enforce Network Level Authentication (NLA), restrict access via firewall rules to authorized IP ranges, use an RDP gateway, and enable account lockout policies.

title: WinRM Service Running
description: Windows Remote Management (WinRM) is running on this system. WinRM allows remote command execution via PowerShell remoting and is a common lateral movement vector used by attackers.
impact: An attacker with valid credentials can use WinRM to execute arbitrary commands remotely. If basic authentication or unencrypted traffic is allowed, credentials may be captured in transit.
remediation_brief: Disable WinRM if not required. If required, enforce HTTPS transport, disable basic authentication, configure TrustedHosts to restrict connections, and monitor WinRM event logs for unauthorized access.

title: SSH Server Enabled
description: An SSH server (OpenSSH) is running on this Windows system. SSH on Windows endpoints is uncommon and may indicate unauthorized installation, developer tools, or a persistence mechanism installed by an attacker.
impact: SSH provides encrypted remote shell access that can be used for lateral movement, tunneling, and persistent access. On Windows endpoints, SSH is rarely business-justified and represents an additional attack surface.
remediation_brief: Disable the OpenSSH Server Windows feature if not required. If required, enforce key-based authentication, disable password login, and restrict access via firewall rules to authorized source IPs.

title: Multiple Remote Management Tools Installed
description: The OpenSSH Server service is running on this Windows endpoint, providing SSH remote access.
impact: OpenSSH on Windows provides command-line remote access. While potentially legitimate for administration, it adds an additional remote access vector that should be documented and monitored.
remediation_brief: If OpenSSH is authorized, ensure it is configured securely: disable root login, use key-based authentication, limit allowed users, and monitor SSH logs. If not authorized, disable the sshd service.

title: End-of-Life Software Installed
description: Software that has reached end-of-life and no longer receives security updates is installed on this endpoint.
impact: EOL software accumulates unpatched vulnerabilities over time with no vendor fixes available. Publicly known exploits continue to work indefinitely. This represents a permanent and growing security gap.
remediation_brief: Upgrade or replace end-of-life software with supported versions. If no replacement is available, implement compensating controls (network isolation, application whitelisting) and document the risk acceptance.

title: Remote Access Software Installed
description: An installed software version is known to contain security vulnerabilities with available updates.
impact: Running known-vulnerable software versions exposes the system to exploits targeting those specific vulnerabilities. Attackers routinely scan for known vulnerable software versions using automated tools.
remediation_brief: Update the software to the latest patched version. If updates are not immediately possible, implement compensating controls such as network segmentation and application-level monitoring. Prioritize based on CVSS score and network exposure.

title: Suspicious Startup Item
description: Development tools (compilers, debuggers, IDEs, scripting language interpreters beyond what the system requires) are installed on a production system.
impact: Development tools enable an attacker to compile and run custom tools directly on the compromised system, create sophisticated payloads, and debug security controls. Their presence on production systems violates hardening baselines.
remediation_brief: Remove development tools from production systems. If development work is needed, use separate development environments. Document any exceptions with business justification and compensating controls.

title: P2P/Torrent Software Installed
description: Software not included in the organization's approved software list was detected. This finding requires per-engagement policy configuration.
impact: Unauthorized software may introduce vulnerabilities, licensing issues, or compliance violations. It may also indicate shadow IT or user-installed tools that bypass change management.
remediation_brief: Review unauthorized software with the system owner to determine if it should be added to the approved list or removed. Implement application control policies (AppLocker, WDAC) to prevent installation of unapproved software.

title: SQL Server Using Mixed Authentication Mode
description: SQL Server is configured with mixed authentication mode, allowing both Windows and SQL Server authentication. SQL authentication transmits credentials that may be weaker and harder to audit than Windows/Kerberos authentication.
impact: Mixed mode enables SQL logins (like 'sa') which are frequently targeted by brute-force attacks. SQL passwords are not subject to Active Directory password policies, may be stored in application config files, and bypass centralized authentication controls.
remediation_brief: Switch to Windows Authentication mode unless SQL authentication is strictly required. If mixed mode must remain, disable the 'sa' account, enforce strong passwords on all SQL logins, and enable SQL Server Audit for login events.

title: IIS Running with Default Site
description: IIS is running with the default web site active. The default site exposes server information, may serve default pages, and typically lacks application-specific hardening that production deployments require.
impact: The default IIS site reveals the web server platform, may expose debug pages or sample applications, and often lacks proper access controls. Attackers use default sites to fingerprint the server and find known vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: Remove or stop the 'Default Web Site' if it is not needed. For production sites, create named sites with specific bindings and remove all default content, sample applications, and documentation.

title: Unnecessary Server Roles Installed on Workstation
description: Server roles (DHCP, DNS, AD DS, Hyper-V, IIS, etc.) are installed on this workstation. Server roles on workstations expand the attack surface with services not intended for endpoint use.
impact: Each server role introduces additional listening services, open ports, and potential vulnerabilities. On a workstation, these roles are rarely monitored or patched with the same rigor as production servers.
remediation_brief: Remove unnecessary server roles via Server Manager or DISM. Workstations should not run server infrastructure services unless specifically authorized and hardened.

title: Web Server Running on Endpoint Workstation
description: A web server (IIS, Apache, Nginx, XAMPP, WAMP, etc.) is running on this workstation. Web servers on endpoints are often development installations with default configurations and no hardening.
impact: Web servers on workstations are typically unmonitored, lack WAF protection, may expose sensitive development data, and are frequently misconfigured with directory listing, debug modes, or default credentials enabled.
remediation_brief: Remove web server software from workstations. Use dedicated servers or containerized development environments. If a local dev server is required, ensure it binds only to localhost (127.0.0.1).

title: End-of-Life Windows Version
description: The Windows operating system version running on this endpoint has reached end-of-life and no longer receives security updates from Microsoft.
impact: An attacker can exploit publicly disclosed vulnerabilities that will never be patched, leading to full system compromise. The organization also faces compliance violations as most frameworks require supported software.
remediation_brief: Upgrade the operating system to a currently supported version of Windows that receives regular security updates. For Windows Server environments, plan a migration path to Server 2019 or later. For desktop systems, upgrade to Windows 10 22H2 or Windows 11. Coordinate with application owners to verify compatibility before migration.

title: Missing Critical Security Updates
description: The endpoint has critical or important security updates pending installation, leaving known vulnerabilities unpatched.
impact: Attackers can exploit publicly known vulnerabilities with available patches. Delayed patching is one of the most common vectors for ransomware and lateral movement within enterprise networks.
remediation_brief: Install all pending critical and important security updates immediately. Configure Windows Update or WSUS to automatically download and install security updates on a regular schedule. Establish a patch management process with a maximum 30-day window for critical updates and 90 days for important updates.

title: Windows Update Service Disabled
description: The Windows Update service (wuauserv) is disabled or stopped, preventing automatic security update installation.
impact: Without the update service running, the system will not receive security patches, accumulating vulnerabilities over time. This creates a growing attack surface that adversaries can exploit.
remediation_brief: Enable the Windows Update service by setting its startup type to Automatic and starting the service. Verify that Group Policy is not overriding this setting. If WSUS or SCCM is used for update management, ensure the client agent is properly configured and communicating with the update server.

title: WSUS Not Configured
description: No Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) or equivalent centralized update management solution is configured for this endpoint.
impact: Without centralized update management, there is no visibility into the patch compliance status of this endpoint. Updates depend on individual machine settings, making enterprise-wide patch compliance difficult to enforce and verify.
remediation_brief: Configure a centralized update management solution such as WSUS, SCCM, or Intune. Point this endpoint to the organization's WSUS server via Group Policy (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows Update > Specify intranet Microsoft update service location).

title: System Uptime Exceeds 90 Days
description: The system has been running for over 90 days without a reboot, which may indicate that kernel-level patches requiring a restart have not been applied.
impact: Many Windows security updates require a system restart to take effect. Extended uptime suggests these updates have been downloaded but not fully installed, leaving kernel-level vulnerabilities unpatched.
remediation_brief: Schedule a maintenance window to restart the system and apply any pending updates that require a reboot. Establish a regular reboot schedule aligned with the organization's patch management cycle, typically monthly following Patch Tuesday.

title: No Windows Backup Configured
description: No Windows backup solution (Windows Server Backup, System Restore, or third-party backup) is configured on this endpoint.
impact: Without backups, data loss from ransomware, hardware failure, or accidental deletion is unrecoverable. This significantly increases the business impact of any destructive attack or system failure.
remediation_brief: Configure Windows Server Backup or a third-party backup solution to perform regular system state and data backups. Store backups on a separate, isolated storage target. Test backup restoration procedures regularly to ensure recoverability.

title: Last Backup Older Than 30 Days
description: The most recent backup on this system is older than 30 days, indicating that backup jobs may have failed or been disabled.
impact: A stale backup means up to 30+ days of data would be lost in a disaster recovery scenario. Critical business data, configuration changes, and system state captured after the last backup cannot be restored.
remediation_brief: Investigate why backups have not completed recently. Check backup job schedules, storage target availability, and backup service health. Resume regular backup operations and configure alerting for backup failures.

title: BitLocker Not Enabled
description: BitLocker Drive Encryption is not enabled on one or more fixed drives, leaving data at rest unprotected.
impact: If the device is stolen or a hard drive is physically removed, all data on unencrypted volumes is accessible without authentication. This includes cached credentials, local databases, documents, and application data.
remediation_brief: Enable BitLocker Drive Encryption on all fixed drives. Use TPM+PIN for pre-boot authentication where possible. Store recovery keys in Active Directory or a centralized key management solution. For systems without TPM, use USB key-based or password-based protectors.

title: TPM Not Available or Not Ready
description: No Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is available or the TPM is not in a ready state on this endpoint.
impact: Without a functional TPM, hardware-rooted security features such as BitLocker with TPM-based protectors, Credential Guard, and Measured Boot cannot be used. The system must rely on software-only security mechanisms which are more susceptible to tampering.
remediation_brief: If the hardware supports TPM, enable it in the BIOS/UEFI firmware settings and initialize it through the TPM Management console (tpm.msc). For virtual machines, enable virtual TPM through the hypervisor. If the hardware does not support TPM, consider hardware replacement during the next refresh cycle.

title: Secure Boot Not Enabled
description: UEFI Secure Boot is not enabled on this endpoint, allowing unsigned or tampered boot components to execute during system startup.
impact: An attacker with physical access or kernel-level privileges can install a bootkit or rootkit that loads before the operating system, persisting across reinstalls and evading all OS-level security controls including antivirus and EDR.
remediation_brief: Enable Secure Boot in the system's UEFI firmware settings. Ensure the operating system was installed in UEFI mode (not legacy BIOS). Verify that all boot components (bootloader, kernel, drivers) are properly signed. Note that enabling Secure Boot on a legacy BIOS-installed system requires OS reinstallation in UEFI mode.

title: Built-in Administrator Account Enabled
description: The built-in Administrator account (RID 500) is enabled on this endpoint.
impact: The built-in Administrator is a well-known target for brute force attacks and cannot be locked out by default. If compromised, it provides full system control. Attackers specifically target this account during password spraying and pass-the-hash attacks.
remediation_brief: Disable the built-in Administrator account and create named individual admin accounts. If the built-in account must remain enabled for emergency access, rename it and set a complex password stored in a password vault. Consider implementing LAPS for local admin password management.

title: Guest Account Enabled
description: The built-in Guest account is enabled on this endpoint, allowing unauthenticated or minimally-authenticated access.
impact: The Guest account provides a foothold for unauthenticated access to the system. Even with limited privileges, it can be used for local enumeration, accessing public shares, and as a stepping stone for privilege escalation.
remediation_brief: Disable the Guest account immediately: net user Guest /active:no. Verify via Group Policy that it remains disabled.

title: Password Never Expires on User Account
description: The local Administrators group contains more than 3 members, indicating excessive administrative access.
impact: Each local administrator account is a potential credential for full system compromise. Excessive admin accounts increase the attack surface for pass-the-hash, credential theft, and privilege abuse. Lateral movement is easier when admin credentials are widespread.
remediation_brief: Review the local Administrators group and remove unnecessary members. Implement the principle of least privilege using standard user accounts for daily operations. Consider implementing LAPS and just-in-time admin access solutions.

title: Excessive Local Administrators
description: One or more interactive user accounts have the 'Password never expires' flag set.
impact: Passwords that never expire may remain unchanged for years, increasing the window for compromise through credential theft or brute force. Compliance frameworks universally require periodic password rotation.
remediation_brief: Remove the 'Password never expires' flag from interactive user accounts. Implement a maximum password age policy (60-90 days). Service accounts should use managed service accounts (gMSA) or be documented with compensating controls if password expiry would break functionality.

title: Weak Password Policy
description: The local password policy does not meet security baselines: minimum length is less than 8 characters and/or password complexity requirements are disabled.
impact: Weak password policies allow users to set easily guessable passwords. Short passwords without complexity requirements can be cracked in seconds using modern hardware, making brute force and dictionary attacks trivially successful.
remediation_brief: Set minimum password length to at least 12 characters and enable complexity requirements. Configure via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies > Password Policy. Consider implementing a password filter or Azure AD Password Protection to block common passwords.

title: Account Lockout Not Configured or Too Permissive
description: The account lockout threshold is set to 0 (disabled), allowing unlimited failed login attempts without locking the account.
impact: Without account lockout, attackers can perform unlimited password guessing attacks against all accounts without triggering any lockout defense. Password spraying and brute force attacks can continue indefinitely.
remediation_brief: Configure account lockout policy: set lockout threshold to 5-10 failed attempts, lockout duration to 30 minutes, and reset counter after 30 minutes. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies > Account Lockout Policy.
